newsitem.title: INDIA: India to place broadcast bill in parliament.
newsitem.headline: India to place broadcast bill in parliament.

text.p: The Indian government plans to introduce a bill in parliament on Friday aimed at opening up the broadcasting sector but regulate foreign television broadcasters.

"We needed a broadcasting law. All leading democracies have already enacted their own broadcasting laws. India needs to have one," information and broadcasting minister S. Jaipal Reddy told Reuters on Thursday.
Asked how foreign broadcasters would be affected, Reddy said: "The idea is not to ban foreign channels or make it difficult for them but to regulate," Reddy said.
The bill has to be passed by parliament before it takes effect.
The bill, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, said a large number of satellite television channels were beaming their programmes into India homes.

"This is more or less a working draft which will be referred perhaps to a joint select committee where senior members belonging to all parties will resolve among themselves to work out a national consensus," Reddy said.
He said lawmakers were worried that Indian firms were denied a level playing field in competition with foreign firms.

The bill said: "All these channels are foreign entities and their programmes are uplinked from outside the country without any regulation through the law of our land, while Indian entrepreneurs and Indian companies are not at present permitted to own either radio or television stations."
India began opening up key sectors under an economic liberalisation programme launched in 1991, but the state still owns radio and television stations.
Currently, private broadcasters can rent time slots and their content is monitored. There are dozens of such slots, mainly for entertainment programmes.
Foreign satellite broadcasters, led by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp-owned Star TV, currently beam their programmes into India from Hong Kong and other centres.
The government plans to grant licences to all broadcasters currently beaming into India, but they will need to bid for licences to provide direct-to-home services (DTH).
The bill proposed to set up an independent authority, to be called the Broadcasting Authority of India, to facilitate and regulate broadcasting services.
Nobody will be allowed to broadcast without a licence, it added, and outlined the terms and conditions for obtaining a licence.
The Broadcasting Authority will grant licences for terrestrial and satellite radio and television broadcasting, direct-to-home broadcasting, local delivery services and other related services.
Indian firms will be granted both terrestrial and satellite broadcast rights but foreign participation in terrestial broadcast services is barred.
Only broadcasters that uplink from within India will be allowed to broadcast in the country, the bill said.
Foreign companies will be allowed to uplink from India only in partnership with Indian firms, and will be allowed to hold only up to 49 percent equity.
The bill also placed curbs on ownership of more than one medium and proposed to restrict newspaper publishing houses from extending their hold to radio and television.
Owners of one medium would be allowed to hold only up to 20 percent of the equity in a single firm of another medium but could hold scattered stakes of less than five percent in several media.
